# Game Design Document for AI_Hell

## Problem statement

The AI_Hell repository is a fresh start with no game content: it consists only of a README (which plans for a `docs/Game Design Document.md` and frames the project as an AI-framework tutorial) and workflow tooling. There is no design document, so neither human developers nor AI agents have an authoritative specification describing the game to build. This work item produces that document: a fully detailed Game Design Document (GDD) for **AI_Hell**, a 2D bullet hell game loosely based on Galaxians.

## Users

- **Human developers** following the README tutorial — need enough specification to implement the game without guesswork, while leaving space for AI/creative input.
- **AI agents** (coding assistants, Context Hub agents) — need a machine-readable, unambiguous specification with precise mechanics (movement, collision, bullets, waves, power-ups, scoring) so they can plan and implement against it.
- **Technical target audience** — the game is an AI-framework demonstration project, written for a technical audience; the GDD is a reference/tutorial artifact, not a commercial pitch.

### Example user stories

- As a **developer/AI agent**, I want the core gameplay loop defined precisely (enemy formations as the bullets, player movement, firing, power-up activation, enemy-fired projectiles in the pre-boss wave) so I can implement a coherent vertical slice.
- As a **developer/AI agent**, I want an explicit MVP scope (5 levels, 1 boss, 3 lives, ≥6 power-ups, local leaderboard, no difficulty scaling) so I can plan and estimate work.
- As a **developer**, I want a code-first technical architecture section that compares 2–3 code-first game engine options (no UI-heavy engine such as Godot/Unity) targeting web + Windows binary, so I can choose and set up the stack.
- As a **reader**, I want a Tron-inspired neon vector aesthetic defined so all art/UI decisions are consistent.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC1 — GDD artifact exists and covers game identity:** The document is created at `docs/Game Design Document.md` and opens with game identity: working title AI_Hell, genre (2D top-down bullet hell, Galaxians-inspired), a one-sentence pitch, target audience, and the Tron-inspired neon vector aesthetic direction.
- [ ] **AC2 — Core gameplay loop fully specified:** The document precisely specifies: formation waves whose enemies are themselves the collision threat ("the enemies are the bullets") in the first levels, with enemy-fired projectiles added in later levels; full 2D player movement (WASD/arrow keys); auto-fire; and Space as the activator for a movement-style power-up (e.g., dash/teleport). The GDD must be explicit that the **final wave of the MVP — the wave immediately before the boss — is an enemy-fired-projectile level**: it contains a smaller number of enemies than the earlier levels, but those enemies fire bullets in a predictable pattern.
- [ ] **AC3 — MVP vertical-slice content specified:** The GDD specifies a complete MVP vertical slice: **5 levels**, 1 boss encounter, 3 lives, at least 6 distinct power-up types, and a simple local leaderboard (local storage); difficulty scaling is explicitly out of scope for the MVP.
- [ ] **AC4 — Content catalog present:** The document includes catalogs with enough detail to implement: enemy types with formation/dive behaviors and bullet-pattern behavior (enemies-as-bullets vs. enemy-fired bullets, including the predictable pre-boss firing pattern), wave structure per level, the boss design, power-up list with effects, scoring system, and level progression.
- [ ] **AC5 — Technical architecture section:** The document specifies a code-first architecture that must run on the web and be distributable as a Windows binary, including: an engine policy (no engine with an extensive UI/editor such as Godot or Unity; code-first game engine libraries such as Phaser are allowed and encouraged), **2–3 concrete engine options with pros and cons for each**, a recommended stack, proposed module/file breakdown, entity/bullet/wave data model, save-data design (local storage), and key technical risks. The precise engine selection is left to the implementors.
- [ ] **AC6 — Validation:** The GDD is reviewed and accepted by the operator (producer review) against the interview answers captured in the clarifying-questions appendix; each major design decision is traceable to an answered question or a documented assumption.
- [ ] **AC7 — Documentation updated:** All related documentation is updated to reflect the changes, including code comments, README, and any relevant wiki or docs site entries (at minimum, README references to the GDD must match the new file).
- [ ] **AC8 — Test suite:** Full project test suite must pass with the new changes (a documentation-only change; run any existing checks/lint as applicable).

## Constraints

- The game must **run on the web** and be **distributable as a binary on Windows**.
- **Engine policy:** no engine with an extensive UI/editor (e.g., Godot or Unity). A **"code-first" game engine library (e.g., Phaser) is explicitly allowed and encouraged**. The precise engine selection is an implementor decision; the GDD must present 2–3 engine options with pros and cons for each.
- This is a **tutorial/demonstration project** for AI-assisted development (Context Hub), not a fully releasable commercial game; scope is a vertical slice.
- Working title is **AI_Hell**; genre is **2D bullet hell, loosely based on Galaxians**.
- MVP scope is fixed: **5 levels**, 1 boss, 3 lives, ≥6 power-ups, local leaderboard; **no difficulty scaling in the MVP**.
- Aesthetic: **neon vector, Tron-inspired**.

## Existing state

- Repository contains only `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, `.gitignore`, `.githooks/`, and `.worklog/` — no game code or design content.
- `README.md` already plans for a `docs/Game Design Document.md` and documents the work-item workflow (Idea → Intake → Plan → In Review → Release). It frames the game as "a classic Bullet Hell game written to demonstrate the use of the Context Hub AI framework... written by humans for a technical target audience."
- No existing work items related to the game design (this item is the first).

## Desired change

A comprehensive GDD at `docs/Game Design Document.md` that enables both humans and AI agents to **guide the development of the game in a consistent way** - an authoritative design reference for all subsequent game development work items. The document is a **living document**: it may be edited during development as the game evolves, and such changes are expected to be tracked in the worklog so decisions remain traceable.

## Key Files

- `docs/Game Design Document.md` — **the deliverable**; new comprehensive design document (identity, core loop, MVP scope, content catalogs, technical architecture with engine options, risks).
- `README.md` — verify/update references so the tutorial points to the correct GDD path (minor).

## Technical architecture recommendation (proposed assumption, to be confirmed at planning)

Engine policy: **code-first only** — no engine with an extensive UI/editor (e.g., Godot, Unity). Code-first game engine libraries are allowed and encouraged; final selection is the implementors' decision. The GDD must present the following options with pros and cons:

1. **Phaser (TypeScript/HTML5)** — pro: mature 2D game framework with scenes, physics, tweens, and input out of the box; large ecosystem and docs; fast to scaffold, ideal for a tutorial. Con: opinionated framework layer over the raw game loop; some abstraction to learn.
2. **PixiJS + hand-written game loop (TypeScript)** — pro: rendering-focused WebGL library, maximum code control, excellent for teaching the game loop/entity systems by hand. Con: no built-in scene/physics/collision — more boilerplate.
3. **Plain HTML5 Canvas + TypeScript (no game library)** — pro: zero dependencies, maximum didactic value for an AI-framework tutorial. Con: input, loop, collision, and rendering all hand-rolled; slowest to build.

Distribution: package the same web codebase as a **Windows binary with Tauri v2** (lightweight, code-first) or Electron (heavier). **Persistence:** `localStorage` for the MVP leaderboard and save data.

## Related work

- `README.md` (repository root) — project framing and tutorial context; planned GDD path.
- No related worklog work items; this item is the seed for all subsequent game work.

## Risks and assumptions

- **Scope creep risk:** the GDD must stay a vertical-slice specification; extra opportunities (difficulty scaling, online leaderboards, more levels, online multiplayer) should be recorded as linked future work items, not added to the MVP.
- **Engine selection:** the concrete engine (Phaser vs. PixiJS vs. plain Canvas, among code-first options) is an implementation decision; the GDD must document 2–3 options with pros/cons, and selection may vary during planning as long as the code-first/web + Windows binary constraints hold.
- **"Enemies are the bullets" ambiguity risk:** the document must crisply define the collision/lethality model (player dies on contact with enemies in early waves; bullets become a secondary threat later, notably in the predictable-pattern pre-boss wave) so implementations do not diverge.
- **AI creativity pacing:** per README guidance, the GDD should nail the core loop in detail while leaving reasonable space for AI suggestions in non-core areas (e.g., art details, pattern variations).

## Appendix: clarifying questions & answers

- Q1: "Gameplay structure — how 'loosely' based on Galaxians? ... player movement — horizontal-only lanes, or free 2D movement?" — Answer (user): "Lets have enemies in formation waves that are themselves the bullets. In later waves the enemies may also fire bullets, but in the first levels they are the bullets. The player has full 2d movement." Source: interactive reply (round 1). **Revised (final accepted answer):** see Q7 — the enemy-fired-bullets capability is made explicit as the final pre-boss wave of the MVP.
- Q2: "Theme & fiction — what does 'AI_Hell' mean narratively? ... And what visual aesthetic ...?" — Answer (user): "I really like your proposal. Lets go with that. In terms of visual aesthetic I think we need to go with a neon vector approach inspired by Tron." Accepted fiction: hellscape ruled by rogue/berserk AI constructs; player pilots a ship through an AI-generated underworld; enemies are literal AI manifestations. Source: interactive reply (round 1).
- Q3: "Scope & structure for a tutorial/demo game ... how many stages for the MVP vision?" — Answer (user): "The MVP should be a vertical slice of the proposed game. Lets say 3 levels, a single boss, 3 lives, at least 6 kinds of power up, leaderboard. We don't need difficulty scaling in the MVP." Source: interactive reply (round 1). **Revised (final accepted answer):** 5 levels — see Q8.
- Q4: "Technology target — should the GDD target a specific stack ... or stay engine-agnostic?" — Answer (user): "You can choose the technical stack. The requirements are that it must run on the web and be distributable as a binary on Windows. We should not use Godot or another such engine, lets focus on a code-first approach." Source: interactive reply (round 2). **Revised (final accepted answer):** see Q9 — "no engine" clarified to mean no UI-heavy engine (Godot/Unity); code-first engines (e.g., Phaser) are explicitly allowed.
- Q5: "Controls & input — keyboard/mouse/gamepad?" — Answer (user): "WASD/Arrow keys, auto-fire, space as an activator for a movement powerup (e.g. dash, teleport from danger)." Source: interactive reply (round 2).
- Q6: "Leaderboard persistence — simple local leaderboard, or online via a backend?" — Answer (user): "simple local storage is sufficient for the MVP." Source: interactive reply (round 2).
- Q7: "AC2 — can we be explicit about enemy-fired projectiles? Should the final wave of the MVP (before the boss) be such a level?" — Answer (user): "Yes — the final wave of the MVP (before the boss) will have such a level. There will be a smaller number of enemies in this level, but they will fire bullets in a predictable pattern." Source: interactive reply (revision round). Prior answer (Q1) left the enemy-firing capability as "later waves may fire bullets"; final accepted answer makes the pre-boss wave an explicit enemy-fired-projectile level with fewer enemies and predictable firing patterns.
- Q8: "AC3 — how many levels should the MVP have?" — Answer (user): "Increase the number of levels to 5." Source: interactive reply (revision round). Prior answer (Q3): 3 levels; final accepted answer: 5 levels.
- Q9: "'No engine' / 'code-first' could be misread as banning game engine libraries — clarify engine policy?" — Answer (user): "We don't want to use an Engine with an extensive UI (e.g. Godot or Unity), but we do want to leverage a 'code-first' engine (e.g. Phaser). The precise engine selected is up to the implementors. Present 2-3 options listing the pros and cons of each." Source: interactive reply (revision round).

- Q10: "Desired change says the GDD will let agents build 'without further clarification' - is that too restrictive?" - Answer (user): "Yes - too restrictive and unrealistic. The goal is a document that will enable agents and humans to guide development of the game in a consistent way. The document itself should be considered a living document and may be edited during development." Source: interactive reply (revision round). Prior text: 'without further clarification'; final accepted answer: consistent-guidance goal + living-document status.

# Settle engine selection on Phaser — remove engine options B and C from GDD

## Problem statement

The Game Design Document (§6.2 Engine Options) currently presents three engine options — A: Phaser (TypeScript/HTML5, recommended), B: PixiJS + hand-written game loop, C: Plain HTML5 Canvas — and explicitly leaves final engine selection to the implementors. The operator has decided to settle on Phaser here and now: options B and C must be removed and Phaser locked in as the definitive engine choice.

## User story

As the game owner, I want the engine decision locked to Phaser so implementation can proceed without engine-choice ambiguity.

## Desired change

Update `docs/Game Design Document.md` (and any related references) so Phaser is the selected engine, not one of several options:

- §6.2 Engine Options: remove Option B (PixiJS) and Option C (Plain HTML5 Canvas); present Phaser as the sole/selected engine; remove the "> Final engine selection is an implementor decision" note and any "can be replaced with Option B or C" text.
- §6.7 risk table: reword the "Engine selection lock-in" entry (choice is now locked; the decoupling mitigation remains).
- §9 appendix decision #4: update to reflect a single code-first engine selected (Phaser), removing the PixiJS/plain-Canvas listing.
- Parent work item AH-0MT7O8KCY0059RA5 AC5 wording ("2–3 concrete engine options... precise engine selection is left to the implementors") conflicts with this decision — update it to reflect Phaser as the locked selection.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC1**: `docs/Game Design Document.md` §6.2 contains Phaser as the sole engine choice; Option B (PixiJS) and Option C (Plain HTML5 Canvas) are removed.
- [ ] **AC2**: The GDD no longer leaves engine selection to implementors — Phaser is stated as the selected/locked engine wherever the engine choice is mentioned (§6.2, §6.7 risk entry, §9 appendix).
- [ ] **AC3**: No stale references to PixiJS or the plain-Canvas option remain anywhere in `docs/` or `README.md` (grep for "PixiJS" and "Option C"/"Plain HTML5 Canvas").
- [ ] **AC4**: Parent work item AH-0MT7O8KCY0059RA5 AC5 (and its child write-GDD AC6 wording where applicable) is updated so it no longer requires 2–3 engine options or leaves selection to implementors — consistent with the locked Phaser decision.
- [ ] **AC5**: All related documentation is updated to reflect the change (GDD sections above, README if it references engine options).
- [ ] **AC6**: Full project test suite must pass with the new changes (docs-only change; run any existing checks/lint as applicable).

## Constraints

- Engine policy stays code-first (no UI-heavy engines like Godot/Unity) — Phaser qualifies.
- Must still run on the web and be distributable as a Windows binary.
- Related work items: parent AH-0MT7O8KCY0059RA5 (Game Design Document for AI_Hell); sibling AH-0MT7URFNN004Z01L (Remove combo bonus from GDD and clarify lives model), similar GDD-edit task.

## Key Files

- `docs/Game Design Document.md` — §6.2 Engine Options, §6.7 risks table, §9 appendix decision #4 (primary edit targets).
- `README.md` — check/update if engine options referenced.
- Parent work item AH-0MT7O8KCY0059RA5 — AC5 wording update.

## Appendix: clarifying questions & answers

- Q: "Which engine option(s) should remain in the GDD?" — Answer (operator rgardler): "Remove options b and c for the engine options. Lets settle on Phaser here and now." (priority medium, operator-specified via /intake). Source: interactive directive. Final accepted: Phaser is the sole engine choice; options B (PixiJS) and C (plain Canvas) removed; engine selection no longer left to implementors.
- Q (answered by research, no user input needed): Where do the 3 options appear? — Answer (Map): §6.2 Options A/B/C (lines 226–258), §6.7 risk row l.404, §9 appendix decision #4 l.465; PixiJS/plain-Canvas strings exist only in `docs/Game Design Document.md` per repo grep. Source: grep of repo.

# Bring simple audio effects into MVP scope (GDD revision) — AH-0MT7UW0Y80062NU1

## Problem statement

The Game Design Document (`docs/Game Design Document.md`) currently excludes audio from the MVP vertical slice: §7.3 is titled "Audio Direction (Out of Scope for MVP, Noted for Future)" and §8 ("Future Scope (Out of MVP)") lists "Sound and music — Full audio implementation". The operator has decided this cannot stand: **simple audio effects must be part of the MVP**, covering all interactions, impacts, and enemy actions, and audio must signal key events **in advance** (telegraphing).

## Users

- **Players** — need immediate, unambiguous audio feedback for every interaction and impact so the game feels responsive without reading the screen.
- **Players** — need advance audio cues for key events (boss entrance, phase shifts, pattern-based enemy fire, dive-bomb attacks, wave/power-up spawns) so they can anticipate and react in a bullet-hell game where threats arrive fast.
- **Developers / AI agents** — need a precise, machine-readable SFX specification (event → sound character, volume, lead time) so the audio system can be implemented without design guesswork.

### Example user stories

- As a **player**, I want a distinct sound when I collect a power-up or activate my dash so my action is acknowledged.
- As a **player**, I want audio for impacts (my ship hit, enemy destroyed, boss damaged) so I can track combat state even peripherally.
- As a **player**, I want audio for enemy actions (spawn, fire, dive) so I can react to threats I may not have visually registered yet.
- As a **player**, I want key events — boss entrance/phase changes, Level-5 Phaser firing cycles, dive-bomb attacks, wave spawns, power-up spawns — announced by a cue **before** the event, so I can prepare.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC1 — GDD §7.3 rewritten: audio in scope for MVP with procedural synthesis:** §7.3 is rewritten to place simple audio effects **in scope for the MVP** and specifies: **procedural synthesis via the Web Audio API** (zero external audio assets; code-generated neon "blips/zaps/hums"); a simple **SFX event catalog** covering all interactions (power-up pickup, dash activation), impacts (player hit, enemy destroyed, boss phase damage, bullet impact), and enemy actions (spawn, fire, dive); and **background music explicitly a nice-to-have / out of MVP scope**.
- [ ] **AC2 — Advance telegraphing specified:** The GDD specifies that key events are announced by an **advance audio cue** with a defined minimum lead time (≥ 500 ms before the event): boss entrance, boss phase transitions (per §4.3's existing "audio cue" promise), E4 Phaser predictable firing cycles (§4.1), dive-bomb attacks, wave spawns, and power-up spawns. This applies in §2 (core loop), §4 (catalogs), and §7.3 (audio), with consistent wording.
- [ ] **AC3 — Consistency pass across the GDD:** §8 "Future Scope" no longer lists sound/music wholesale out of scope — SFX is removed from that list; music remains future/nice-to-have (entry reworded or annotated). §6.4 `src/audio/AudioManager.ts` and §6.6 `ai_hell_settings` (sound volume) entries are confirmed/updated — including a **master/SFX volume setting and a mute toggle** — and §6.7 risks gains an entry for the **browser autoplay policy** (AudioContext must be created/resumed after a user gesture; mitigation: init audio on first input/menu interaction) plus SFX **rate-limiting/spam control** for high-frequency events (e.g., auto-fire).
- [ ] **AC4 — Validation:** The GDD revision is reviewed and accepted by the operator (producer review) against the documented assumptions; each design decision is traceable to an interview answer or a documented assumption.
- [ ] **AC5 — Documentation updated:** All related documentation is updated to reflect the changes, including code comments, README, and any relevant wiki or docs site entries (verify README references are consistent with the revised GDD).
- [ ] **AC6 — Test suite:** Full project test suite must pass with the new changes (documentation-only change; run any existing checks/lint as applicable).

## Constraints

- Game must **run on the web** and be distributable as a **Windows binary** (Tauri); the audio approach must work in both.
- **Code-first engine policy**; Phaser is the locked engine choice (sibling item AH-0MT7UTPH3001B6IE) — Phaser's built-in audio support (Web Audio) is available, but the spec must remain engine-agnostic enough to survive if the lock changes.
- **No external audio assets** for the MVP — **procedural Web Audio API synthesis only** (operator decision).
- **Simple** — "simple audio effects": crisp, digital, neon-style sounds; not a full audio pipeline (no music scoring, voice, ambience, dynamic/adaptive audio).
- **Music is a "nice-to-have"** — not required for MVP; kept out of scope and noted for future.
- **Browser autoplay policy** applies — audio must be initialized after a user gesture (e.g., clicking Start/Play).

## Existing state

- `docs/Game Design Document.md` §7.3: audio direction described but marked **out of scope for MVP** ("Visual feedback (screen shake, flash) can substitute temporarily").
- §8 "Future Scope (Out of MVP)" lists "Sound and music — Full audio implementation".
- §4.3 Boss design already promises "clear telegraphing (glow, charge, **audio cue**) before the attack begins" — an in-scope audio cue contradicts the out-of-scope §7.3.
- §4.1 E4 Phaser: "fires... in predictable, repeating cycles... with clear tell animations" — no audio tell specified.
- §6.4 module breakdown already plans `src/audio/AudioManager.ts — Sound effects and music`.
- §6.6 save-data already defines `ai_hell_settings` = "Sound volume, control bindings" — needs volume + mute detail.
- §6.2/§6.7: no audio-related risk entries; engine lock-in item (AH-0MT7UTPH3001B6IE) is in progress.

## Desired change

A surgical revision of `docs/Game Design Document.md`:

1. **Rewrite §7.3** → "Audio Direction (MVP: In Scope — Simple SFX)": procedural Web Audio synthesis approach; SFX event catalog (interactions, impacts, enemy actions) with sound character guidance (neon blips/zaps/hums, pitch/volume hints); background music marked nice-to-have/out-of-MVP; advance telegraphing requirement with ≥ 500 ms lead time.
2. **Update §8**: remove SFX from future scope; keep/reword "music" as future/nice-to-have.
3. **Consistency pass**: §2 core loop (audio feedback), §4.1 E4 tell + audio, §4.3 boss telegraphing (confirm audio cue in scope), §6.4 AudioManager, §6.6 settings (volume + mute), §6.7 risks (autoplay policy, SFX rate limiting).
4. Keep it minimal — no new sections beyond what's needed; no music scoring or asset pipelines.

## Key Files

- `docs/Game Design Document.md` — **the deliverable**; revise §7.3, §8, and cross-references (§2, §4.1, §4.3, §6.4, §6.6, §6.7).
- `README.md` — verify no audio/scope references need updating (minor, if any).

## Related work

- `Game Design Document for AI_Hell (AH-0MT7O8KCY0059RA5)` — parent epic; this item is a child GDD-revision item.
- `Settle engine selection on Phaser - remove engine options B and C from GDD (AH-0MT7UTPH3001B6IE)` — Phaser locks in built-in audio support; relevant to the Web Audio approach.
- `Remove combo bonus from GDD and clarify lives model (AH-0MT7URFNN004Z01L)`, `Clarify enemy pass-through and bullet-blocking rules in GDD (AH-0MT7USMWN0071UF5)` — sibling GDD-revision items; same workflow pattern.
- GDD internal: §4.3 (existing "audio cue" telegraphing promise) is the hook this item resolves.

## Risks and assumptions

- **Browser autoplay policy (medium)** — AudioContext cannot start before a user gesture; audio must initialize on first input/Start click. Mitigation: define init-on-gesture in the GDD; fall back silently until user interacts.
- **SFX spam/cacophony (medium)** — high-frequency events (auto-fire, fast bullet hits) could overlap into noise. Mitigation: per-sound rate limiting/throttle and modest volume; note in GDD.
- **Scope creep (low-medium)** — music, ambience, voice, dynamic/adaptive audio, and asset pipelines invite themselves once SFX is in scope. Mitigation: hard-scope to "simple SFX" per operator; music tracked as nice-to-have only; record extras as linked future work items, not scope.
- **Assumption — deliverable is a GDD revision (docs), not game code** — the repo has no game implementation yet; confirmed by operator (Q1 = "a").
- **Assumption — procedural Web Audio API synthesis, zero external assets** — confirmed by operator (Q2 = "a").
- **Assumption — music out of MVP, nice-to-have** — confirmed by operator (Q3: "music is a 'nice to have'").
- **Assumption — telegraph list accepted** — boss entrance, boss phase transitions, E4 Phaser cycles, dive-bomb attacks, wave spawns, power-up spawns; proposed in round 1, no objection raised.
- **Assumption — Phaser engine lock proceeds** — if AH-0MT7UTPH3001B6IE is not implemented, the Web Audio API spec remains engine-agnostic; Phaser's audio wrapper is a detail.

## Appendix: clarifying questions & answers

- Q1: "The repo has no game code yet — should this be (a) a GDD revision moving simple audio into MVP scope and specifying it precisely (recommended, matches sibling revision items), or (b) a feature implementation item (no game code exists to attach it to)?" — Answer (user): "a". Source: interactive reply (round 1). Final accepted answer: GDD revision, docs work item.
- Q2: "Which audio asset approach should the GDD specify for the MVP — (a) procedural synthesis via Web Audio API (zero assets, code-generated neon blips/zaps/hums, fits code-first policy and Phaser's built-in audio), (b) small bundled CC0 audio files, or (c) no preference/implementor decision?" — Answer (user): "a". Source: interactive reply (round 1). Final accepted answer: procedural Web Audio API synthesis only; zero external assets.
- Q3: "Keep background music out of the MVP (SFX only), or also specify a simple looping synthwave track?" — Answer (user): "music is a 'nice to have'". Source: interactive reply (round 1). Final accepted answer: music is not required for the MVP; SFX-only scope, music noted as nice-to-have/future.
- Q4: "Proposed advance-telegraphing targets: boss entrance, boss phase transitions, E4 Phaser predictable firing cycles, dive-bomb attacks, wave spawns, power-up spawns — confirm or adjust?" — Answer (user): no objection raised after the round-1 interview; accepted as proposed (documented assumption; recorded as OPEN QUESTION if operator wants to adjust lead-time or event set).
## Related work (automated report)

### Related work items
- **AH-0MT7V5UH90023XWR** – Clarify enemy health / one-hit destruction model in GDD (open)
- **AH-0MT7UY5UR002LD5U** – Redesign P7 Dash: make collectable teleport power-up (in-progress)
- **AH-0MT7URFNN004Z01L** – Remove combo bonus from GDD and clarify lives model (in-progress)

### Repository file matches
- `docs/Game Design Document.md` — matched: advance, audio, context, create, design (+22 more)
- `README.md` — matched: case, context, create, design, docs (+14 more)
- `AGENTS.md` — matched: bring, cannot, case, context, create (+13 more)

# Add an extra life power up

## Problem statement

The AI_Hell GDD (§4.4) defines 7 power-up types (P1–P7) and a fixed 3-life per-run model with no continue mechanic. There is no way for a player to gain additional lives during a run, which limits player agency and recovery from mistakes in later levels.

## Users

- **Players** of the AI_Hell game — benefit from a high-value, rare power-up that extends their run and reduces frustration from a single mistake in later levels.
- **AI agents / human developers** implementing the game from the GDD — need the power-up specified precisely (drop rarity, stacking rule, activation) so implementations do not diverge.

### Example user stories

- As a **player**, I want to occasionally collect an extra life drop from destroyed enemies so I can survive longer in difficult levels.
- As a **player**, I want to know extra lives are rare and capped, so the power-up feels special and doesn't trivialize the 3-life challenge.
- As a **developer**, I want the extra-life power-up defined in the GDD catalog with drop rate and cap rules so I can implement it without guesswork.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC1 — GDD power-up catalog updated:** The power-up catalog in `docs/Game Design Document.md` §4.4 gains a new entry **P8 – Extra Life** (collectible, passive, applies immediately), consistent with the existing P1–P7 table format (ID, name, effect, icon suggestion).
- [ ] **AC2 — Lives mechanics spec updated:** The GDD's lives mechanics (game-over/lives references) specify that collecting P8 adds **+1 life** up to a **maximum of 5 lives**; excess pickups have no effect at the cap.
- [ ] **AC3 — Drop rarity specified:** The GDD specifies that the extra-life power-up drops at a **lower rate than standard power-ups (~5% per destroyed enemy)** while standard power-ups keep their existing ~15–20% drop rate.
- [ ] **AC4 — Consistent count references:** Any GDD statements about power-up counts (e.g., "6+ distinct types" in §4.4 and the MVP content summary in §3) remain accurate with the addition (e.g., "7+ distinct types" or equivalent); the MVP "3 lives" starting value is unchanged.
- [ ] **AC5 — Validation:** The updated GDD is reviewed and accepted by the operator against the clarifying-questions appendix; the design decision (5-life cap, ~5% drop, passive) is traceable to an answered question.
- [ ] **AC6 — Documentation updated:** All related documentation is updated to reflect the changes, including code comments, README, and any relevant wiki or docs site entries.
- [ ] **AC7 — Test suite:** Full project test suite must pass with the new changes.

## Constraints

- The GDD is the authoritative design artifact in this repository (no game code exists yet); the change is a documentation/design change to `docs/Game Design Document.md`.
- The GDD is a **living document** — edits are allowed and expected, tracked in the worklog.
- MVP starting lives stay at **3**; the **max cap is 5**.

## Existing state

- GDD §4.4 defines power-ups P1–P7 (P7 Dash is a permanent Space-activated core ability, distinct from temporary pickups).
- Power-ups drop from destroyed enemies with a **random chance of ~15–20% per enemy** (stated in the §4.4 intro).
- The player has **3 lives per run, no continue mechanic** (§3); game ends when out of lives (§2/game-over rules).
- No existing worklog item covers extra-life or additional power-ups.

## Desired change

Add a rare, passively collected **Extra Life** power-up (P8) to the GDD: collected by flying over it (like all pickup power-ups), instantly grants +1 life, capped at 5 lives total. It drops at a reduced rate (~5%) compared to standard power-ups. No activation key involvement (unlike P7).

## Key Files

- `docs/Game Design Document.md` — **the deliverable**; update §4.4 power-up table (add P8), §4.4 intro drop-rate wording (rare exception for extra life), and any lives-mechanics / MVP-content references (§2, §3) to reflect the 5-life cap and extra-life pickup.

## Related work

- `docs/Game Design Document.md` (repository root of the design) — the document being changed; see §4.4 Power-Ups, §3 MVP content, §2 core loop.
- Work item "Game Design Document for AI_Hell" (AH-0MT7O8KCY0059RA5) — created the GDD and its clarifying-questions appendix.
- Work item "Write the Game Design Document" (AH-0MT7QQGBU008V4R0) — implemented the GDD.
- Work item "Remove combo bonus from GDD and clarify lives model" (AH-0MT7URFNN004Z01L) — clarifies that a hit by any object removes a life; complementary to this item (extra lives restore the same pool). Both edit `docs/Game Design Document.md`; merge-order awareness needed (related-to, not blocking).
- Work item "Settle engine selection on Phaser - remove engine options B and C from GDD" (AH-0MT7UTPH3001B6IE) — unrelated to this change (engine section), surfaced by related-work scan.

## Risks and assumptions

- **Scope-creep risk:** keep the change minimal — one new power-up entry plus consistent references; do not add related features (e.g., life-up stacking UI, per-life bonuses) to this item; record extras as linked work items.
- **Balance assumption:** the ~5% drop rate and 5-life cap are the operator's chosen values; if playtesting later shows imbalance, adjust via a separate work item.
- **Count-reference consistency:** updating "6+" to "7+" must not accidentally change MVP starting lives or the "3 lives" stat.
- **No code exists yet:** implementers of the eventual game must be able to derive exact behavior (instant passive +1, cap at 5) from the GDD alone.

## Appendix: clarifying questions & answers

- Q1: "Drop rarity — extra life is more valuable than other power-ups. Should it have a lower drop chance (e.g., ~5% per enemy) than standard power-ups?" — Answer (operator): "yes". Source: interactive reply.
- Q2: "Max lives cap — can extra lives stack beyond the starting 3? If so, should there be a cap (e.g., max 5)?" — Answer (operator): "max 5". Source: interactive reply.
- Q3: "Activation — is it collected passively with instant effect (+1 life), or needs an activation key (like P7 Dash / Space bar)?" — Answer (operator): "passive". Source: interactive reply.

data.description:
# Redesign P7 Dash: make collectable teleport power-up

## Problem statement

The Game Design Document (§4.4) currently describes P7 (Dash) as a permanent, always-available ability activated by Space, unique among all power-ups in that it cannot be collected. This violates the game's design principle that all power-ups are collectables dropped by enemies, and the "dash" behavior is not what the developer wants: P7 should teleport the player instead and be renamed **Teleport**.

## Users

- **Player** — wants a movement escape tool that gets them out of danger reliably (teleport to a safe spot), rewarded via collection like every other power-up.
- **Developer/AI agent** — wants an unambiguous spec commit: P7 becomes a collectable, Space-activated teleport with safe-spot resolution and a P6 buff on arrival, so the code can be written without guessing.

### Example user stories

- As a **player**, I want to collect a Teleport power-up from a destroyed enemy so I can press Space to escape to a safe spot in the direction I'm travelling.
- As a **player**, I want to be intangible for a moment after I reappear (P6 Phase Shift) so I am never killed at my landing spot.
- As a **developer**, I want P7 to be exactly like P1–P6 (collectable, no permanent abilities) so there is one uniform power-up model.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC1 — Collectable, not permanent:** §4.4 removes P7's "*(Space-activated, permanent)*" designation and its accompanying uniqueness note; P7 is documented as a collectable power-up dropped by enemies like P1–P6, with no always-available core ability.
- [ ] **AC2 — Teleport, not dash:** P7 is **renamed Teleport** and its effect documented as a **teleport** (not a dash): pressing Space while holding a Teleport teleports the player in the direction of travel to a **safe location** — the engine searches for the nearest safe spot (free of enemies and bullets) along the travel direction, clamped to screen bounds. If no safe spot exists in the travel direction, the player teleports to the nearest on-screen position anyway (safety guaranteed by the P6 buff, see AC4).
- [ ] **AC3 — Single-use, stackable:** Each collected P7 grants one teleport use, consumed on activation; collecting multiple P7s stacks multiple teleports (one use per collection). Priority of use is earliest-collected-first (FIFO).
- [ ] **AC4 — P6 on reappearance:** Upon reappearing after a teleport, the player gains the Phase Shift effect (intangibility, passes through enemies and bullets) for safety, as defined for P6.
- [ ] **AC5 — Docs consistency and rename:** All GDD references align with the new design — P7 is renamed **Teleport**; §2.1 controls table (Space activates the movement power-up only while held), §2.3 power-ups note, §4.4 table and note, app architecture (`Dash.ts` → `Teleport.ts`, no longer "always active"), and the controls reference in §8 (Space for dash power-up → teleport power-up).
- [ ] **AC6 — Testing/validation:** The GDD is reviewed for internal consistency (no lingering "permanent", "always active", or "dash away from nearest enemy" language); all existing documentation remains accurate.
- [ ] **AC7 — Documentation:** All related documentation updated to reflect the changes, including code comments, README, and any relevant wiki or docs site entries.
- [ ] **AC8 — Test suite:** Full project test suite must pass with the new changes.

## Constraints

- No permanent power-ups exist in the game — P7/Teleport must conform to the existing collectable model (random drop chance ~15–20% per enemy, §4.4).
- Space remains the activation mechanism for movement-type power-ups, but it only works while the player holds at least one Teleport.
- Teleport destination must be on-screen (clamped to screen bounds) and safe (no enemies/bullets at destination).
- MVP scope unchanged (5 levels, 1 boss, 3 lives, 6+ power-ups).

## Existing state

- §2.1 controls: **Space** → "Activate movement power-up (dash/teleport away from nearest threat)".
- §2.3: "**Space bar** activates the movement-type power-up (see §4.4)".
- §4.4 table P7: **Dash** *(Space-activated, permanent)* — "Press Space to dash/teleport away from the nearest enemy in the opposite direction; 3-second cooldown".
- §4.4 note: P7 is unique — "always available… not a temporary power-up but a core ability that is always active", may be visually enhanced (e.g., Speed Boost increases dash distance).
- App architecture: `Dash.ts` — P7 (always active); controls reference §8: "Space for dash power-up".

## Desired change

- P7 renamed to **Teleport**. Collectable like P1–P6.
- Space (while a teleport is held) → teleport player in the direction of travel to the nearest safe spot, clamped to screen bounds; if no safe spot exists, teleport to nearest on-screen position anyway. Single use per collected power-up; stackable (FIFO).
- On arrival, apply P6 Phase Shift effect (intangibility ~3 seconds) to guarantee safety.
- Remove dash behavior, cooldown, "away from nearest enemy" logic, and all permanent-ability language.

## Key Files:

- `docs/Game Design Document.md` — §2.1 controls table (line ~32), §2.3 power-ups note (line ~46), §4.4 power-ups table + P7 note (lines ~164–167), app architecture `Dash.ts` → `Teleport.ts` (lines ~297–298), §8 controls reference (line ~468).

## Related work

- AH-0MT7O8KCY0059RA5 — Game Design Document for AI_Hell (source of the current P7 spec)
- AH-0MT7QQGBU008V4R0 — Write the Game Design Document
- AH-0MT7UX8LE0072MR3 — Add an extra life power up (sibling §4.4 power-up catalog edit; also touches power-up catalog)
- AH-0MT7URFNN004Z01L — Remove combo bonus from GDD and clarify lives model (sibling GDD edit)
- AH-0MT7USMWN0071UF5 — Clarify enemy pass-through and bullet-blocking rules (sibling GDD edit)
- AH-0MT7UW0Y80062NU1 — Bring simple audio effects into MVP scope (sibling GDD edit)
- AH-0MT7V5UH90023XWR — Clarify enemy health / one-hit destruction model (sibling GDD edit)
- AH-0MT7UTPH3001B6IE — Settle engine selection on Phaser (sibling GDD edit; architecture section)

## Risks & assumptions

- **Assumption:** "Direction of travel" means the player's current movement vector at the moment Space is pressed (last non-zero movement direction if stationary).
- **Assumption:** P6 Phase Shift applied on arrival is the full P6 effect (3-second intangibility).
- **Scope creep:** Spec additions beyond the GDD text (e.g., visual/audio teleport FX, movement-power-up UI) are out of scope and should be separate work items.

## Appendix: Clarifying questions & answers

- Q1: "Activation mode — Space-activated or immediate-on-collect like P1–P5?" — Answer (user): "Yes [Space-activated]." Source: interactive reply (round 1).
- Q2: "Usage model — single use vs. time window with cooldown?" — Answer (user): "single, though the player can collect multiple teleport powerups and stack them." Source: interactive reply (round 1).
- Q3: "What is a 'safe location'?" — Answer (user): "safe spot [engine searches for nearest safe spot in the direction of travel, free of enemies/bullets, clamped to screen bounds]." Source: interactive reply (round 1).
- Q4: "Keep the name 'Dash' or rename to 'Teleport'?" — Answer (user): "rename to Teleport." Source: interactive reply (round 2).
- Q5: "Fallback when no safe spot exists in the travel direction?" — Answer (user): "teleport anyway [to nearest on-screen position, relying on the P6 buff]." Source: interactive reply (round 2).
